paper_claims.claim: The term structure of equity returns is downward-sloping: stocks with high cash flow duration earn 1.10% per month lower returns than short-duration stocks in the cross-section (equal-weighted decile sorts, July 1963-June 2014).
Factor models can explain only part of the return differential: the D1-D10 strategy earns a FF3 alpha of 0.84%, FF4 (3F+MOM) alpha of 0.66%, and FF5 alpha of 0.48% per month, all highly significant.
The duration premium is three times larger after periods of high investor sentiment, and excess returns of high-duration stocks load positively on changes in the Baker-Wurgler sentiment index.

Analysts extrapolate past earnings growth: LTG forecasts are twice as high for high-duration stocks and shrink by more than 50% over five years, while realized growth is similar; high-duration stocks have negative earnings surprises; price-target implied returns do not vary with duration.

The duration premium is concentrated in short-sale constrained stocks (low residual institutional ownership, 1.32%/month) and disappears for unconstrained stocks (0.15%/month, insignificant); the pattern holds within size and book-to-market bins.

The duration premium is robust: stable across 11 parameter variations, an out-of-sample pre-estimation sort, five subsamples, and is even larger for volatility-managed portfolios whose factor-model alphas are essentially unaffected.
